lectures.name: Introduction to MCC Clinical Presentations
lectures.title: Introduction to MCC Clinical Presentations
lectures.framing: The Medical Council of Canada organises medicine around clinical presentations — what the patient walks in with — rather than diagnoses. The one idea: sort a presentation by how specific it is to one body system and how urgent it is.
lectures.keypoints: A sign is found by the practitioner on PEx; a symptom is what the patient perceives as abnormal for them. Undifferentiated presentations (fatigue, malaise) point to no one system; single typical ones (abdominal pain, knee swelling) do. Life-threatening presentations are handled by the ABCs first. Preventive care (pap test, fecal blood test, glucose, lipids) is itself a presentation.

blocks.html:
Signs vs symptoms
  • Sign: what the health care practitioner identifies on PEx
  • Symptom: what the patient perceives as “not normal” for them

lectures.name: Tasks of a Physician 1 - Patient-Centered Approach
lectures.title: Tasks of a Physician 1 - Patient-Centered Approach
lectures.framing: The frameworks a physician uses to structure an encounter — from the patient-centred clinical method and the diagnostic pathway through prescribing, prevention and ethics. The organising idea: every step attends to both the disease and the person's illness experience.
lectures.keypoints: Check stability and vitals first, then Hx → PEx → Ix → DDx → Tx. FIFE (feelings, ideas, function, expectations) explores the illness experience. VITAMIN C&D generates a DDx. Choosing Wisely: least invasive test first, and only tests that change management. The prevention paradox: population-wide prevention brings large community benefit but little to each individual. The four physician-patient models run from informative (technical expert) to paternalistic (guardian).

blocks.html:
Patient-centred clinical method
  1. Exploring both disease and illness experiences – Hx, PEx, Ix, FIFE
  2. Understanding the whole person – proximal (modifiable) and distal (non-modifiable) contexts
  3. Finding common ground – problems, goals, roles, mutual decisions
  4. Incorporating prevention and health promotion
  5. Enhancing the patient-physician relationship
  6. Being realistic
FIFE – the illness experience
  • Feelings – How does your disease/symptom make you feel?
  • Ideas – What do you think is wrong?
  • Function – How are your symptoms impacting your function/enjoyment of life?
  • Expectations – What do you hope to get out of the medical visit?

Microbiology – infection work-up: bacteria, viruses, yeast, parasites
Hematology – blood cells and elements, clotting parameters

blocks.html:
ABCDE of ordering investigations
  • Acquire – prepare for the sample/specimen/test
  • Be aware – know collection techniques (container, fixative, PtID, order the test)
  • Communicate – talk to the lab, patient, and family
  • Diagnose – interpret the report/results
  • Expedite – contact lab/imaging (urgent or not)

blocks.html:
Choosing Wisely Canada
  1. Consider the least invasive testing option first
  2. Only order tests which will change patient management
  3. Discuss and educate patients on whether tests are necessary
  4. Seek clarification if you believe something was ordered unnecessarily
  5. Do NOT recommend tests exclusively for the learning experience
  6. Do NOT recommend tests in anticipation of preceptor preference
ADL and IADL
  • Activities of daily living (ADL): feeding, dressing, bathing, walking – deficits may indicate a need for home healthcare/nursing facility
  • Instrumental activities of daily living (IADL): cooking, cleaning, transportation, laundry, managing finances – improve QOL
The 4 Ps
  • Predisposing: put an individual at risk of developing a problem
  • Precipitating: a specific event/trigger to the onset of the current problem
  • Perpetuating: maintain the problem once it has become established
  • Protective: strengths of the individual that reduce the severity of the problem

WHO 6 steps of rational prescribing
  1. Patient's problem – symptoms, diagnosis, patient characteristics
  2. Therapeutic objective – curative, symptomatic, preventive
  3. Treatment choice – contraindications, interactions, comedications
  4. Start treatment – write Rx
  5. Give patient information – instructions, warnings
  6. Monitor treatment – continue, adjust, stop

blocks.html:
Approaches to disease prevention and control
  • Clinical / individual-centred approach – causes of cases
  • Public health / population-based approach – causes of disease incidence
  • High-risk strategy – seeks to identify high-risk susceptible individuals
  • Population strategy – seeks to control the determinants of incidence and lower the mean level / shift the distribution of risk factors
  • Prevention paradox: prevention that brings large benefits to the community offers little to each participating individual

blocks.alt: Staircase diagram: upstream social and economic determinants, individual behaviours, chronic conditions, chronic disease, disability and death, over the life course
blocks.cap: The chronic disease continuum. Upstream determinants → individual behaviours (risk factors) → chronic conditions (risk conditions) → chronic disease → disability and death, over the life course.

blocks.html:
Risk vocabulary
  • Risk: probability that a specific action/exposure will give rise to a negative health outcome
  • Risk factor: individual characteristics or behaviours that increase the likelihood that a person will suffer negative health outcomes – smoking, alcohol, diet, physical activity
  • Risk condition: chronic condition that contributes to risk of disease/disability/death – obesity, hypertension, pre-diabetes, high cholesterol/BP, metabolic syndrome
  • Multimorbidity: co-existence of 2+ chronic conditions
  • Co-morbidity: an index disease holds priority over other co-occurring chronic diseases

blocks.html:
Ethical theories
  • Deontology / Kantianism – based on pure reason and duty; never treat others merely as a means to an end
  • Utilitarianism – maximize utility and minimize bad
  • Principlism / pluralistic theory – autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice
  • Casuistry – bottom-up reasoning; inferring from similar past cases
  • Narrative ethics – reflection and drawing broader lessons; personal identity and storytelling; highly contextual/subjective
  • Feminist / communitarian ethics – critical of mainstream bioethics that neglects women's issues/perspectives
  • Pragmatism – looks for a 3rd “outside the box” solution
  • Virtue ethics – focused on the character of the individual; pursue eudaemonia; balance character traits between vices
Practical ethical decision-making
  1. Recognition – gather and manage appropriate data considering the relevant values
  2. Designation – clarify the goals and describe the ethical conflict
  3. Evaluation – explain why this problem exists, distinguish the cause, and highlight ethical issues
  4. Clarification – evaluate the feasible options and identify the implications
  5. Determination – decide the “best” solution to the problem
  6. Implementation – take action, with an established evaluation process

lectures.name: Tasks of a Physician - Applying Frameworks
History of Medicine
lectures.title: History of Medicine
lectures.framing: How medicine moved from the humoral theory to the germ theory, and the figures who made the physician a diagnostician. The organising idea: disease explained by natural causes, not religion or magic.
lectures.keypoints: Humoral theory: blood, yellow bile, black bile, phlegm. Germ theory's program: identify the organism → develop a lab diagnostic test → discover a chemotherapeutic agent. Hippocrates rejected religious/magical healing; Galen set Hippocratic medicine in an anatomy and physiology framework.

blocks.html:
Theories of disease
  • Humoral theory: blood, yellow bile, black bile, phlegm
  • Germ theory: identify the micro-organism, develop a laboratory diagnostic test, discover a chemotherapeutic agent
Key figures
  • Hippocrates – rejected religious/magical healing; introduced the medical practitioner as a diagnostician/therapist
  • Galen – took clinical Hippocratic medicine and set it within a wider anatomy and physiology framework

lectures.name: Cultural Competence in Health Care and the Care of Refugees
lectures.title: Cultural Competence in Health Care and the Care of Refugees
lectures.framing: Cultural competence as a continuum running from destructiveness to proficiency, then what the WHO says every clinician should know about refugee and migrant health. The organising idea: moving along the continuum means recognising differences and acting on them, not treating everyone the same.
lectures.keypoints: Cultural blindness (treating everyone the same) is still low on the continuum – it meets only the dominant group's needs. Cultural humility: our own perspective is not the only, or necessarily the “correct”, one. Refugees/migrants are generally healthy, have lower risk of all cancers except cervical, but more diabetes and more PTSD than the host population; labour migrants are the largest group.

rows: Forced assimilation, subjugation, rights and privileges for dominant groups only
Racism, maintained stereotypes, unfair hiring practices

blocks.html:
Related concepts
  • Cultural safety: fostering an environment that is spiritually, socially, and emotionally safe
  • Cultural humility: recognition that our own perspective is not the only and not necessarily the “correct” perspective

10 things to know about the health of refugees and migrants (WHO)
  1. The health of refugees/migrants is important – a basic human right
  2. The numbers of migrants are often overestimated
  3. Refugees/migrants are likely to be healthy in general
  4. They can face challenges accessing health care – legal status, language barriers, discrimination
  5. Lower risk for all forms of cancer, except cervical cancer, but more diabetes than the host population
  6. Breakdown in health systems in the country of origin
  7. PTSD seems more prevalent among refugees and asylum seekers than the host population
  8. Labour migrants are the largest group of migrants globally – more work-related injuries
  9. Children without parents or a guardian are especially vulnerable
  10. Making health systems refugee- and migrant-friendly

lectures.name: Muscle Tissue
lectures.title: Muscle Tissue
lectures.framing: Basic biochemistry and histology, the three muscle types and the sarcomere, the cells of the nervous system, and the body's fluid compartments. The organising idea: structure predicts function – striations, nuclei and fibre shape tell you which muscle you are looking at and how it behaves.
lectures.keypoints: Skeletal = striated, voluntary, multinucleated (peripheral nuclei); cardiac = striated, involuntary, single central nucleus, intercalated disks; smooth = not striated, spindle-shaped. During contraction the I band and H zone shorten and the sarcomere shortens (the A band does not). Schwann cells myelinate one segment of one axon (PNS); oligodendrocytes myelinate many axons (CNS). TBW = 60% of body weight: ICF 2/3, ECF 1/3; in Darrow-Yannet diagrams the ECF always changes first.

blocks.html:
Biochemistry
  • DNA – double-stranded, relatively stable, thymine (methyl group)
  • RNA – single-stranded, degrades quickly, uracil, translated into proteins
  • Micromolecules – monosaccharides, fatty acids, glycerol, nucleotides, amino acids, minerals, water, cofactors, vitamins

blocks.html:
Histological stains
  • Hematoxylin: basic stain that stains acids blue; basophilic structures – DNA, RNA, ribosomes
  • Eosin: acid stain that stains bases pink; acidophilic structures – cytoplasmic proteins, muscle

blocks.html:
The sarcomere and the sliding filament model
  • I band = isotropic; divided by a Z line (disc)
  • A band = anisotropic; divided by an H zone and M line
  • Sarcomere = Z line to Z line; the functional unit of muscle
  • I bands and H zones shorten during contraction; sarcomeres shorten
  • Troponin complex = T-troponin (tropomyosin binding), I-troponin (inhibitory – binds actin), C-troponin (calcium binding)
  • Tropomyosin = binds actin and blocks myosin binding in the absence of Ca2+

blocks.alt: Micrograph of a sarcomere with Z lines, thin and thick filaments, I band and A band labelled
blocks.cap: One sarcomere runs Z line to Z line; the A band is the length of the thick filaments, the I band is thin filament only.

blocks.alt: Diagram of a sarcomere relaxed (top) and contracted (bottom)
blocks.cap: Relaxed vs contracted: thin filaments slide over thick filaments, so the I band and H zone narrow while filament lengths stay the same.

blocks.html:
Neurons
  • Motor neurons (efferent) – multipolar; convey impulses from brain, spinal cord, and ganglia to effector cells
  • Sensory neurons (afferent) – pseudo-unipolar or bipolar, in ganglia; convey impulses from receptors to the CNS
  • Integrative neurons (interneurons) – multipolar; form integrating networks between sensory and motor neurons
  • Axonal transport on microtubules is needed to deliver vesicles to the synapse
  • Neurons do NOT divide, but peripheral nerves can repair: sprouts are generated and Schwann cells re-innervate the muscle
Myelination
  • Schwann cells (PNS) – one cell myelinates only a segment of a single axon
  • Oligodendrocytes (CNS) – one cell myelinates many axons
  • Myelin sheath = concentric layers of lipid membranes and proteins that insulate the axon
Nervous system supporting cells
  • Astrocytes – scaffolded network in the CNS between capillaries, fibres, and neurons; maintain the blood-brain barrier
  • Microglia – transform into phagocytic cells in damaged CNS; defence system; migratory
  • Ependymal cells – simple epithelial lining of the ventricles and spinal canal; ciliated to propel CSF

Homeostatic control systems
  • Sensors – detect changes and transmit an input signal
  • Integrating centres – process the information
  • Effectors – receive and process the output signal

blocks.html:
Body fluid compartments
  • TBW = total body water = 60% of body weight
  • ICF = intracellular fluid (K+) – 2/3 of TBW
  • ECF = extracellular fluid (Na+, Cl-) – 1/3 of TBW: interstitial fluid 3/4, plasma 1/4
  • Hypo/hypernatremia = Na+ → Addison's disease, diabetes insipidus
  • Hypo/hyperkalemia = K+ → cardiac arrest
  • Hypo/hypercalcemia = Ca2+

blocks.cap: ICF = 2/3 of TBW; ECF = 1/3, of which interstitial fluid is 3/4 and plasma 1/4.

Darrow-Yannet diagrams

  • Changes always occur to the ECF compartment first

lectures.name: Connective Tissue
lectures.title: Types of Connective Tissue
lectures.framing: Connective tissue classified from embryonic mesenchyme through connective tissue proper to the specialized tissues (fat, cartilage, bone, blood-forming tissue), and how its fibres are made. The organising idea: each type is defined by its cells, its fibres (collagen type), and its ground substance.
lectures.keypoints: Loose CT carries vessels and nerves under epithelia; dense regular (tendons, ligaments) = type I collagen in rows for stress resistance. Brown fat = multilocular, many mitochondria, newborn thermoregulation; white fat = unilocular. Cartilage is avascular: hyaline and elastic use type II collagen, fibrocartilage types I and II. Articular hyaline cartilage lacks perichondrium, so regenerates poorly (osteoarthritis). Reticular fibres = type III collagen.

Components of connective tissue

lectures.name: Cellular Communication
lectures.title: Cellular Communication
lectures.framing: How cells hold together, move substances across membranes, signal one another, and fire and transmit an action potential all the way to muscle contraction. The organising idea is a single chain: resting potential → action potential → NMJ → excitation-contraction coupling.
lectures.keypoints: RMP = -70 mV, set mainly by K+ leak; the Na+/K+ pump moves 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in. The AP is all-or-none: threshold -55 mV, peak +45 mV, undershoot to -90 mV. Absolute refractory period = Na+ channels inactivated. At the NMJ, Ca2+ influx releases ACh (more Ca2+ = more ACh); ACh on nicotinic receptors → EPP → muscle AP. In ECC, Ca2+ binds troponin so tropomyosin uncovers myosin-binding sites on actin. Myopathy: normal nerve conduction, reduced muscle amplitude; neuropathy: abnormal conduction.

blocks.html:
Cellular junctions
  • Tight junctions – barrier; establish apical/basolateral domain polarity
  • Adherens junctions – cell-cell adhesion; interlocking cadherin molecules
  • Gap junctions – intercellular communication; connexins intermix and form channels
  • Desmosomes – cell-cell adhesion; snap-like structures attached to intermediate filaments
  • Hemidesmosomes – cell-matrix adhesion; attach intermediate filaments to protein complexes, linking to the basement membrane

rows: Diffusion and filtration; secretes lubricating substances

blocks.html:
Cellular transport
  • Simple diffusion – passive, down the concentration gradient; small lipophilic molecules (O2, CO2, steroid hormones, alcohol)
  • Facilitated diffusion – carrier proteins, down the concentration gradient; larger polar molecules
  • Active transport – carrier-mediated, against the concentration gradient, requires ATP; Na+/K+ pump, Ca2+ pump
    • Primary – energy derived directly from the breakdown of ATP
    • Secondary – uses the potential energy of a gradient generated by primary transport; symport = same direction, antiport = opposite directions
  • Osmosis – movement of water down its concentration gradient
    • Osmolality = # of Osmol/kg of water
    • Osmolarity = # of Osmol/L of solution; ECF osmolarity = 290 mOsM
  • Tonicity: the ability of a solution to cause osmosis across a biological membrane
  • Factors affecting the rate of diffusion through membranes: concentration gradient, lipid solubility, molecular size, membrane area, composition of the lipid layer
Cell signalling
  • Autocrine – cell signals to itself
  • Paracrine – chemical messengers released over relatively short distances
  • Cell-cell contact – intracellular mediators diffuse through gap junctions
  • Synaptic – nerve cells transmit signals via release of neurotransmitters
  • Endocrine – hormones produced by specialized cells are released into the bloodstream and travel to target cells

Resting membrane potential
  • RMP = -70 mV
  • Membrane is highly permeable to K+ and slightly permeable to Na+ and Cl-
  • K+ and Cl- are the most important ions in generating the RMP
  • Leak K+ channels help establish the negative RMP
  • Na+/K+ pump maintains the gradients by moving 3 Na+ OUT and 2 K+ IN
The action potential – terms
  • All-or-none response and unidirectional
  • Depolarization: membrane potential moves towards zero
  • Threshold: voltage at which an action potential is triggered
  • Repolarization: return of the membrane potential to its resting value
  • Hyperpolarization: membrane potential moves to more negative values
  • Absolute refractory period: no stimulus will excite the nerve; voltage-gated (V.G.) Na+ channels inactivated
  • Relative refractory period: a stronger than normal stimulus is required; some V.G. Na+ channels have recovered

blocks.alt: Action potential trace: membrane potential in mV against time in ms, with threshold, depolarization, repolarization and hyperpolarization marked relative to RMP
blocks.cap: Threshold at about -55 mV, peak near +45 mV, then repolarization and an undershoot below RMP before return to -70 mV.

blocks.html:
The action potential – sequence
  1. Stimulate nerve
  2. Membrane depolarizes (-70 mV to -55 mV)
  3. V.G. Na+ channels open very rapidly
  4. Na+ flows into the cell
  5. Action potential is initiated
  6. Membrane depolarizes rapidly to +45 mV
  7. V.G. K+ channels begin opening while V.G. Na+ channels become inactivated
  8. Eventually all V.G. K+ channels are open and all V.G. Na+ channels are inactivated
  9. K+ rushes out of the cell
  10. Membrane repolarizes (+45 mV to -70 mV)
  11. K+ continues to leave the cell as V.G. K+ channels close slowly
  12. Membrane hyperpolarizes to -90 mV
  13. V.G. K+ channels close
  14. Membrane potential returns to normal (-70 mV) and V.G. channels return to resting configuration

blocks.html:
Neuromuscular junction
  • Pre-synaptic axon terminal of the motor neuron – filled with synaptic vesicles
  • Synaptic cleft – space between the pre- and post-synaptic cells
  • Post-synaptic membrane of the skeletal muscle fibre
NMJ transmission and excitation-contraction coupling (ECC)
  1. AP on the motor nerve depolarizes the axon terminal and V.G. Ca2+ channels open
  2. Ca2+ flows in and ACh is released – larger [Ca2+] = more ACh
  3. ACh diffuses across the synaptic cleft to the end plate
  4. ACh binds to nicotinic receptors and chemically gated channels open
  5. Na+ flows into the muscle cell and K+ flows out – local depolarization, so no AP yet
  6. Depolarization causes an end plate potential (EPP)
  7. EPP triggers V.G. Na+ channels to open, triggering an AP
  8. The AP propagates over the sarcolemma and down the T-tubules
  9. Voltage sensors in the T-tubule detect the AP and change shape
  10. The voltage sensor opens Ca2+ channels on the lateral sac of the sarcoplasmic reticulum
  11. Ca2+ binds to troponin, causing tropomyosin to roll off the myosin binding sites on actin
  12. Myosin attaches to actin (crossbridge formation) and the power stroke occurs
  13. Actin (thin myofilaments) slides over myosin (thick myofilaments) and the muscle contracts (sliding filaments)
  • Contraction continues as long as there are stimuli at the NMJ, ACh is available, and Ca2+ is in the sarcoplasm
  • Relaxation – ACh is broken down by acetylcholinesterase and taken back up into the axon terminal; Ca2+ is actively pumped back into the SR by Ca2+ ATPase; tropomyosin covers the myosin binding sites and the muscle relaxes
  • Thin myofilaments – G-actin (myosin binding sites), tropomyosin (covers myosin binding sites), troponin (regulatory protein)
  • Thick myofilaments – many myosin molecules (heads contain actin binding sites and ATP binding sites)

lectures.title: Body System Organization
lectures.framing: Cartilage and bone biology, how the body is organised into regions and systems, the imaging modalities used to see it, and the evidence-based-medicine toolkit for judging studies. The organising idea: know the normal structure, and know how trustworthy the evidence about it is.
lectures.keypoints: Osteoblasts build bone (osteoid); osteoclasts (fused monocytes/macrophages, in Howship's lacunae) resorb it. Intramembranous ossification has no cartilage template (skull, clavicle); endochondral replaces one (long-bone length). CT = x-ray slices, big radiation dose, avoid in pregnancy; MRI: T1 short TE/TR, T2 long TE/TR – fluid bright; MRI is contraindicated with pacemakers, cochlear implants, ferromagnetic implants. Intention-to-treat analyses patients as assigned, not as treated. NNT = 1 / (rate in untreated − rate in treated); power = 1 − β.

blocks.html:
Radiograph (x-ray)
  • Ionizing radiation; need a minimum of 2 radiographs at 90° (anteroposterior, posteroanterior, lateral, oblique)
  • Silhouetting: structures become distinguishable because of the different tissue opacities surrounding them
  • Summation / superimposition: overlapping structures; may mislead the reader into thinking there is an abnormality
  • Cannot differentiate muscles and tendons; cannot visualize the brain or internal joint structures
CT
  • X-rays; thin 3D slices (axial)
  • Voxel: small 2D measurement of volume; accuracy and precision increase the likelihood that small lesions and abnormalities will be detected
  • Can visualize the brain and heart; cannot visualize internal joint structures
  • More expensive; much larger dose of ionizing radiation; not recommended for pregnant women
MRI
  • Powerful magnet and radio waves
  • Echo time (TE): the energy signal received at a specific time after the radiofrequency coil pulse
  • Repetition time (TR): the signals received as the pulse is turned on and off
  • T1-weighted: short TE and TR – show fat best, but are fat-suppressed; mostly grey/black image
  • T2-weighted: long TE and TR – show damaged or pathologic tissue (fluids) best; bright signal
  • Proton density weighted: short TE, long TR – reveal dense tissue well (cartilage, tendon, joint pain)
  • Most expensive, longest time to produce an image
  • Contraindications: cardiac pacemakers, cochlear implants, ferromagnetic metal implants
Ultrasound / sonography
  • High-frequency sound waves
  • Diverse, safe, lowest cost – increasingly used in diagnostic and therapeutic medicine

Evidence-based medicine
  • Evidence-based medicine = clinical judgement + scientific evidence + patient preference and values
  • Clinical significance: value = (the formula did not survive extraction)
  • Medical reversal: a new clinical trial, superior to its predecessors in controls, design, size, or endpoints, contradicts current clinical practice; undermines trust in the medical system
  • Critical appraisal: carefully and systematically assessing the outcome of scientific research to judge its trustworthiness, value, and relevance in a particular context
  • PICO framework: patient/problem/population, intervention, comparison/control/comparator, outcomes

blocks.alt: Levels of evidence pyramid: meta-analyses, RCTs, cohort studies, case-control studies, case series or reports, editorials and expert opinion
blocks.cap: Levels of evidence, top to bottom: meta-analyses → RCTs → cohort → case-control → case series/reports → editorials and expert opinion.

blocks.html:
Study designs
  • Meta-analysis: combines the individual effects of a number of studies addressing the same question to produce a summary effect
  • Randomized controlled trial: subjects allocated to experimental or control group by chance – simple, block, or stratified randomization
  • Prospective cohort: exposure and non-exposure are confirmed as they occur during the study
  • Retrospective cohort: exposure is confirmed from past records
  • Case-control: cases are compared with controls with respect to exposure
    • Incident cases = newly diagnosed; can identify risk factors, but must wait a period of time and excludes deaths
    • Prevalent cases = diagnosed for a period of time; can study right away, but may identify characteristics of survival
  • Cross-sectional: exposure and outcome measured at the same point in time
  • Case report / series: detailed description of one or a few cases without a control group
Blinding
  • Open label – all parties aware
  • Single blind – patient/clinician unaware
  • Double blind – patient + investigator unaware
  • Triple blind – patient + investigator + analysts unaware
  • Unblinding – disclosure of allocation

Bias, analysis and error
  • Confounder: an extraneous variable whose presence affects the variables being studied so that the results do not reflect the actual relationship between them
  • Lead time: the interval between diagnosis by a screening program (preclinical phase) and diagnosis by presentation of signs and symptoms (clinical phase)
  • Intention-to-treat: study groups analysed according to the treatment they were assigned, NOT what they received, if any
  • Per-protocol analysis: only includes patients who completed the treatment they were originally allocated
  • Number needed to treat (NNT): the number of individuals who would need to be treated with the new therapy to prevent one negative outcome; NNT = 1 / (rate in untreated group − rate in treated group)
  • Type I error (α): the sample shows a difference between treatment groups when no difference exists
  • Type II error (β): the sample shows no difference between treatment groups when a difference exists
  • Power: probability of finding a treatment difference when a true difference exists; power = 1 − β
  • One-sided test: investigators suspect a difference in one direction only; two-sided test: unsure of the direction
  • Internal validity – correct study methodology
  • External validity – representativeness of the reference population, generalizability
  • Reliability – intrasubject, intraobserver, interobserver variation
Diagnostic test properties
  • Sensitivity: ability of a test to identify people with disease; positive disease / positive no disease
  • Specificity: ability of a test to identify people without disease; negative no disease / no disease
  • Positive predictive value (PPV): positive disease / (positive disease + positive no disease)
  • Negative predictive value (NPV): negative no disease / (negative disease + negative no disease)
  • Likelihood ratio (LR): ability of a test to change the pre-test into the post-test probability of disease – LR > 10 large change; LR = 1 no change; LR < 1 post-test probability < pre-test; LR < 0.1 large change

lectures.name: Child Development
lectures.title: Child Development
lectures.framing: The well-baby assessment, the red flags of abnormal development, and the theories (attachment, Erikson, conditioning, Piaget) used to describe how a child develops. The organising idea: development follows a predictable sequence, so missing a stage on time – or losing a skill – is the signal.
lectures.keypoints: Use WHO growth charts and correct for prematurity until 24 months if born < 37 weeks. Failure to thrive: weight < 3rd percentile and family norm, or crossing 2 major percentile lines. Loss of previously acquired skills is a red flag at any age; so is hand preference before 2 years. Secure attachment (60-65%) comes from prompt, consistent caregiving; disorganized attachment from frightened/frightening caregiving. Piaget: sensorimotor (object permanence) → preoperational (symbolic play) → concrete operational (conservation) → formal operational (abstract thought).

blocks.html:
Goals of the “well baby” assessment
  1. Growth – length, weight, head circumference; correct age until 24 months if born < 37 weeks gestation; use WHO growth charts
    • Failure to thrive: weight less than 3rd percentile and family norm; weight trajectory crosses 2 major percentile lines
    • Short stature: height less than 3rd percentile and family norm
    • BMI > 85th percentile = overweight; BMI > 95th percentile = obese
  2. Parent/caregiver concerns
  3. Nutrition – feeding, supplementation, stool pattern/urine output
  4. Education and advice – injury prevention, behaviour and family issues, environmental health, other issues
  5. Development – inquiry and observation of milestones
  6. Physical examination
  7. Problems and plans / current and new referrals – medical specialist, dietician, speech, audiology, PT, OT, eyes, dental, social
  8. Investigations/screening and immunization

Theories of development
  • Gesell (1928) – wrote detailed descriptions of normal child development
  • Erikson (1950) – psychosocial development (table below)

  • Skinner – operant conditioning (below)
  • Piaget – cognitive development (table below)

Classical conditioning (Pavlov & Thorndike)
  • Reinforcement: the stimulus-response relationship is strengthened through repeated association
  • Extinction: the stimulus-response relationship is weakened
  • Generalization: the conditioned response becomes linked to a stimulus similar to the initial stimulus
Operant conditioning (Skinner)
  • Positive reinforcement: addition of a positive event that increases the behaviour
  • Negative reinforcement: ending of a negative event that increases the behaviour
  • Punishment: addition of an event that decreases the behaviour
  • Response cost: loss of positive reinforcement that results in decreased behaviour/extinction

lectures.name: Genetics
lectures.title: Genetics
lectures.framing: The vocabulary of genetic variation and the patterns of inheritance, each with its signature pedigree. The organising idea: who is affected, in which generations, and whether males pass it to sons tells you the mode of inheritance.
lectures.keypoints: AD: every generation, both sexes, all forms of transmission (including male-to-male). AR: usually one sibship in one generation; consanguinity ↑ risk; trans compound variants cause disease, cis do not. X-linked: almost only males; no male-to-male transmission; carrier females can be affected by skewed X-inactivation. Anticipation = triplet repeat disorders (fragile X CGG, Huntington CAG, myotonic dystrophy CTG, Friedreich GAA). Gonadal mosaicism explains recurrence of an apparently new dominant mutation (~1%). Mitochondrial disease = maternal inheritance, heteroplasmy, threshold effect.

blocks.html:
Genetics terminology
  • Allelic heterogeneity – different variants in the same gene; different phenotypes
  • Locus heterogeneity – mutations in different genes at different chromosomal loci cause the same phenotype
  • Penetrance – fraction of individuals carrying a gene who manifest a specific phenotype; complete = always shows signs, incomplete = may not show signs
  • Anticipation – symptoms become more apparent/severe with each new generation; triple repeat disorders

lectures.name: Examination of a Well Newborn & Infant
Genetic Screening
lectures.title: Genetic Screening
lectures.framing: When to suspect a genetic disorder, and the screening programs that run from preconception through pregnancy to the newborn. The organising idea: screening tests estimate risk; only invasive tests (CVS, amniocentesis) diagnose.
lectures.keypoints: Suspect a genetic disorder with DD/dysmorphism/malformations, family history, 3+ miscarriages, consanguinity/ancestry, or early/multiple cancers. Folic acid 0.8-1 mg/day from 3 months before pregnancy through the 1st trimester. NT > 3.5 mm → ↑ risk of aneuploidy, CHD, skeletal dysplasia, Noonan. eFTS (11-13w6d) screens T18/T21 at a 1:350 cut-off; NIPT (> 9 wk) screens cell-free placental DNA. CVS 11-13 wk, 1/100 miscarriage; amniocentesis 15-20 wk, 1/200. Ontario newborn screening covers 30 metabolic disorders, mostly AR.

blocks.html:
When to consider a genetic disorder
  • Developmental delays, dysmorphic features, or congenital malformations
  • Positive family history of a genetic disorder
  • History of 3+ miscarriages/stillbirths, infertility, neonatal deaths
  • Consanguinity / ethnic background:
    • Ashkenazi Jewish – Tay-Sachs, BRCA1, Canavan disease, familial dysautonomia
    • French Canadian – Tay-Sachs
    • Mediterranean – β-thalassemia
    • Southeast Asian – α-thalassemia
    • Amish/Mennonite and Arab – various rare disorders
    • African – sickle cell anemia
    • Caucasian – cystic fibrosis
  • Cancers – multiple family members, early onset (< 50), multiple primaries in 1 individual, occurrence in the less commonly affected sex
  • Early-onset heart disease / sudden deaths

Ontario newborn screening
  • Screens for 30 metabolic disorders – most are autosomal recessive
  • Wilson & Jungner criteria: disease (serious, natural Hx understood, asymptomatic stage), screening test (acceptable, economical, reliable), management (treatable, available)
  1. Metabolic diseases – body is unable to break down certain substances in foods
  2. Endocrine diseases – body produces too much or too little of certain hormones
  3. Sickle cell disease (SCD) – affects the movement of oxygen in the blood
  4. Cystic fibrosis (CF) – causes problems with breathing and growth
  5. Severe combined immune deficiency (SCID) – affects the body's ability to fight infections
  6. Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) – causes muscle weakness and wasting
  7. Critical congenital heart disease (CCHD) – affects the quantity of oxygen in the blood
  8. Congenital hearing loss

Preconception counselling
  • Provision of information and support to a couple planning a pregnancy, to promote health and reduce risk
  • Primary prevention – review personal and family Hx and refer if any genetic conditions are present
    • Folic acid 0.8-1 mg/day beginning 3 months prior to pregnancy, continued through the 1st trimester
    • Avoid smoking, alcohol, drugs, and exposure to saunas/heat stress
  • Secondary prevention – discuss options for prenatal screening and diagnosis
Prenatal screening – pros and cons
  • Advantages: anticipatory guidance, decisions about labour and delivery, further diagnostic investigations, in-utero interventions, termination of pregnancy (before 24 weeks)
  • Disadvantages: increased anxiety, knowledge is not necessarily power, inability to enjoy pregnancy, uncertain results, limitations of screening

Nomenclature and classification
  • Karyotype: total number of chromosomes, then sex chromosomes
  • Chromosome groups: A (1-3), B (4-5), C (6-12, X), D (acrocentric chromosomes: 13-15, 21, 22), E (16-18), F (19-20)
  • Microarray: arr(1-22)x2,(XY)x1
  • ACMG variant classes: 1 = pathogenic, 2 = likely pathogenic, 3 = variant of uncertain clinical significance, 4 = likely benign, 5 = benign

Nutrients

lectures.name: Common Childhood Behaviors
lectures.title: Common Childhood Behaviors
lectures.framing: Two halves: the basics of inflammation and immunity (innate vs adaptive, MHC, antibodies, immunization), then a general approach to common childhood behaviours – colic, night waking, tantrums, aggression, school avoidance. The organising idea for behaviour: take a careful Hx and PEx first, then decide typical (anticipatory guidance) vs atypical (further Ax and Tx).
lectures.keypoints: Innate immunity acts within hours via PRRs recognising PAMPs/DAMPs; adaptive immunity develops over time via antigen-specific TCR/BCR and clonal selection.   • Chronic inflammation – tissue remodelling and loss of function over time

lectures.name: Well Child and Adolescent Health Encounters
Social Pediatrics
lectures.title: Social Pediatrics
lectures.framing: Health Canada's social determinants of health, the life-course models of how early adversity shapes later health, and the three levels of intervention. The organising idea: upstream interventions change the causes-of-the-causes; downstream ones change the effects.
lectures.keypoints: Childhood experiences matter: toxic stress alters brain development and ACEs act across the lifespan. Three life-course models: latency (one exposure, effect decades later), accumulation (exposures add up), pathways (early exposure sets off a chain of later adversity). Upstream = macro policy, midstream = micro policy/living conditions, downstream = service-level access.

blocks.html:
Health Canada social determinants of health
  • Income and social status – low income, income inequality, social exclusion
  • Employment and working conditions – safety at work, stress at work, social environment
  • Education and literacy – job opportunities, social-psychological status, healthy lifestyle
  • Childhood experiences – toxic stress alters brain development, negative coping skills, ACEs effects across the lifespan
  • Physical environments – walkability, housing, neighbourhood density
  • Social supports and coping skills – system supports, personal coping style, adverse life events
  • Healthy behaviours – smoking and substance abuse, diet
  • Access to health services – proximity, privileges, competing pressures
  • Biology and genetic endowment – epigenetics, gene-environment interaction, genetic predisposition
  • Gender – discrimination, gender pay gap, childcare responsibilities
  • Culture – religious beliefs, cultural views on illness and health, cultural healing practices
  • Race and racism – vulnerable populations, marginalization, discrimination
Life-course models of childhood experience
  • Latency: exposure at one point in the life course affects health years to decades later, despite any intervening experiences
  • Accumulation: multiple exposures over the life course have individual health effects, but also combine to create more significant effects
  • Pathways: a sequence of exposures in which one stage of life influences the probability of later exposures; the early exposure sets off a pathway towards further adversity

Learning disabilities, behaviour disorders and intellectual disability often surface at school; a specific learning disability requires a significant deficit – 2 grades below expectations.   • Learning disabilities, behaviour disorders, and intellectual disability may become evident during the school years

  • Diagnosing a specific learning disability requires a “significant” academic deficit – 2 grades below expectations

lectures.name: ADHD Primer

lectures.framing: What ADHD is, how it is diagnosed, and how it is treated. The organising idea: the diagnosis needs enough symptoms, for long enough, starting early enough, in more than one setting, with real impairment – and nothing else that explains them better.
lectures.keypoints: 6+ inattentive and/or 6+ hyperactive-impulsive symptoms for ≥ 6 months, several present before age 12, in 2+ settings, with clear functional impairment, and not better explained by another disorder. ADHD is highly heritable. Assessment: parent and child interviews across settings, rating scales (SNAP-IV), psychological tests. Tx: psychoeducation, parent training/behavioural management, school accommodation, stimulants, non-stimulants.

blocks.html:
ADHD
  • Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD): a neurodevelopmental disorder defined by a persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that interferes with functioning or development
  • Causes: highly heritable, gene-environment interaction, neurochemical/structural/functional brain abnormalities
  • Assessment: thorough Hx (parent interview, child interview, consider multiple settings), rating scales (SNAP-IV), psychological tests
  • Tx: psychoeducation, parent training/behavioural management, school accommodation, stimulants, non-stimulants
Diagnostic criteria
  • A. 6+ inattentive symptoms and/or 6+ hyperactive-impulsive symptoms persisting for at least 6 months, inconsistent with developmental level, with direct negative impact on social and academic/occupational activities
  • B. Several symptoms were present prior to age 12 years
  • C. Several symptoms are present in two or more settings – home, school, work, with friends/relatives, other activities
  • D. Clear evidence that the symptoms interfere with, or reduce the quality of, social, academic, or occupational functioning
  • E. Symptoms do not occur exclusively during schizophrenia or another psychotic disorder and are not better explained by another mental disorder – mood, anxiety, dissociative, or personality disorder, substance intoxication, withdrawal

The organising idea: live vaccines give stronger, broader immunity but cannot be given to the immunocompromised, pregnant or neonates; non-live vaccines are safe but need adjuvants and boosters.
lectures.keypoints: Efficacy = controlled studies; effectiveness = real world. The herd-immunity threshold rises with transmissibility – high R0 (measles) needs higher coverage. Live attenuated: measles, OPV, rota, varicella, yellow fever, BCG, oral typhoid. Rotavirus is the only routine oral vaccine in Canada. Measles PEP: vaccine within 72 h if immunocompetent > 6 months; IG within 4-6 days if immunocompromised, pregnant, or < 6 months. HIV PEP within 72 h for 28 days.

blocks.html:
Ideal vaccines
  • Safe with minimal adverse effects
  • Effective – lifelong protection after a single dose that can be given at birth
  • Inexpensive
  • Stable during shipment and storage
  • Easy to administer
What vaccines do
  • Individual level – protect the immunized person against the specific disease
  • Population level – reduce the incidence of disease; reduce exposure of susceptible individuals and consequent illness
  • Vaccine efficacy: ability to prevent illness in people vaccinated in controlled studies
  • Vaccine effectiveness: ability to prevent illness in people in the real world
Herd immunity
  • Herd immunity: the immunity of a population against a specific infectious disease
  • A population's resistance to spread depends on the percentage of people who are immune and the probability that those still susceptible will contact an infected person
  • The proportion that must be immune depends on the transmissibility of the agent – from a symptomatically infected person or an asymptomatically colonized person
  • High R0 = highly infectious diseases that require higher immunization coverage – measles
